idea: A patent-style drawing of the Malling-Hansen writing ball, its keys standing up from a brass hemisphere like a pincushion, captioned with Nietzsche's line, typed on one in 1882: 'Our writing tools are also working on our thoughts.' A strange, beautiful machine and a quote that fits every new tool, from the typewriter to the chatbot.

An anatomy plate of a goose quill cut for writing, labelled barrel, shoulder, slit and nib, with a small folding knife beside it and the caption 'Penknife (n.): the knife you cut your pen with.' The everyday word is a fossil of the quill era, which is a sharp, tidy fact to wear.

A fine-line world map with two routes for one drink: dotted sea lanes carrying 'te' (thé, Tee, tea) out of coastal Fujian, and solid overland caravan routes carrying 'cha' (chai, çay, chá) across Asia, captioned 'Te came by sea. Cha came by land.' The Min Chinese word spread by Dutch ships and the Mandarin and Cantonese word by land, so the map is real linguistics and a lovely graphic.

Hymen Lipman's 1858 patent drawing of a pencil with an eraser fixed to one end, labelled 'U.S. Patent No. 19,783', with a footnote: 'Priestley, 1770: it rubs out pencil marks. Hence "rubber".' A clean drawing of an object that plans for mistakes, and a true word origin to go with it.

An anatomy-plate dog in profile with callout lines from its mouth to the same bark in eight languages: woof (English), wan wan (Japanese), meong meong (Korean), wang wang (Mandarin), wau wau (German), guau guau (Spanish), hav hav (Turkish), gav gav (Russian), captioned 'Same dog.' It's warm and funny, with a serious point: even onomatopoeia is a convention you have to learn.

The Egyptian hieroglyph for 'scribe' (Gardiner sign Y3) drawn large, with leader lines naming its parts: palette with two ink wells, water pot, reed pen, all tied together by a cord, captioned 'sš: to write. Drawn as the kit.' The sign for writing is a picture of the tools for writing, which is elegant and quietly funny.

Three Chinese characters drawn in growing size like a botanical progression: 木 'tree', 林 'grove', 森 'forest', with the trunks and branches traced faintly behind each stroke and the caption 'One tree. Two trees. A forest.' It's a tiny, true lesson in how characters are built, and it hangs nicely beside the Haeckel and seed-head shirts.

A technical key to an Inca khipu: a main cord with hanging strings, its three knot types drawn and labelled (single knots for tens and hundreds, long knots for units, figure-eight knot for one), and one string decoded as '352', captioned 'Khipu. Records kept in knots, base ten.' Andean officials did keep accounts this way, and it widens the reader's idea of what counts as writing.

Melvil Dewey's ten main classes drawn as a radial chart of ten drawers, from '000 General works' to '900 History & geography', each with a tiny icon, captioned 'Everything, in ten drawers. 1876.' Dewey published the system in 1876, and the shirt is for librarians and anyone who likes the audacity of filing all knowledge.

A letter-evolution strip showing the Old English thorn þ in manuscript, then its blackletter form, then its slow merger into a 'y' as early printers made do without it, ending with 'Ye Olde', captioned 'Pronounced "the".' It's a fact that quietly ruins every fake-medieval sign, which is exactly what this crowd likes.

A cutaway plate of an oak marble gall, showing the gall wasp larva in its chamber, beside a small recipe diagram: crushed galls + iron sulphate + gum arabic = black ink, captioned 'Iron gall ink. Written in a wasp's nursery.' Most medieval manuscripts, and much writing until the 20th century, used this ink, so it's natural history and book history in one plate.

A botanical plate of the papyrus sedge with a cross-section of its stem and an exploded diagram of a sheet: pith cut into strips, one layer laid across the other at right angles, pressed and dried, captioned 'Before paper: two layers of reed. (And the word.)' The word 'paper' comes from 'papyrus', and the construction is beautifully simple.

A redrawn engraving of Agostino Ramelli's 1588 book wheel, a rotating reading machine with books held open on its shelves and gears that keep them level, captioned 'Many tabs open. 1588.' A gorgeous Renaissance machine with a sly modern caption for anyone who reads ten things at once.

Thomas Edison's 1876 patent drawing of his electric pen, a motorised needle meant for punching stencils to copy office documents, captioned 'Built to copy letters. Became the tattoo machine.' Samuel O'Reilly's 1891 tattoo-machine patent was based on Edison's design, which is a great twist for a shirt.

A specimen ladder of one word set in increasing sizes, each labelled with its old name and approximate point size: Agate 5½, Nonpareil 6, Brevier 8, Long Primer 10, Pica 12, English 14, Great Primer 18, captioned 'Before points, type sizes had names.' The names were real printers' terms, and they read like a little poem.

The word 'knight' with every letter given its Middle English sound in a phonetic line underneath (/kniçt/), arrows showing the k and the gh falling silent over the centuries, captioned 'Every letter used to work.' It explains English spelling in one word, for people who've always wondered why it's so strange.

A contour map of La Gomera with a whistled sound wave drawn from one ridge to another across a ravine, captioned 'Silbo Gomero. Spanish, whistled.' Islanders really do talk across valleys by whistling Spanish, and UNESCO listed the practice as intangible heritage in 2009. It's a language turned into landscape.

A schematic of the Diamond Sutra scroll from Dunhuang, its frontispiece and colophon labelled, with the colophon's own words: 'for universal free distribution', and the date '868'. It's the oldest dated printed book known, and its first printed message is about giving the text away, which is a point of view worth wearing.

A cutaway diagram of a paper wasp nest, its grey layered walls labelled 'chewed wood fibre', captioned 'Réaumur, 1719: wasps make paper from wood. Why don't we?' He suggested it to the French Academy, and wood-pulp paper took over more than a century later, so it's a nature plate about patience and noticing.

Two small semaphore figures, one holding its flags for N and one for D, with dotted lines showing how the two shapes overlap into the peace symbol, captioned 'Nuclear Disarmament. Gerald Holtom, 1958.' The world's best-known protest sign is literally two letters, and few people know it.
